CHEM 3400H
Section 01

UV-Vis and Diode Array Detection

01
CHEM 3400H

UV detection and Beer's law

A = εlc
  • Light passes through the flow cell.
  • The detector measures the light absorbed by the analyte.
  • At fixed wavelength and path length: absorbance increases with concentration.
  • Use the relationship only within the validated linear range.
CHEM 3400H

One wavelength, or the whole spectrum at once?

Fixed-wavelength UV

  • One selected wavelength
  • Simple, fast, and sensitive
  • No spectral identity information

Diode array (DAD)

  • Many wavelengths at once
  • A spectrum across each peak
  • Useful for spectral comparison
CHEM 3400H

Choosing a detection wavelength

  • Choose a wavelength near the analyte's absorbance maximum.
  • Stay above the solvent's UV cutoff.
  • Check for absorption by the mobile phase and sample matrix.
No useful chromophore? Expect weak or no UV response.
CHEM 3400H

DAD can flag possible co-elution

  • Compare spectra at the leading edge, apex, and tail.
  • Matching spectra support a single component.
  • Changing spectra suggest possible co-elution.
Peak-purity output supports an assessment. It does not prove purity.
CHEM 3400H

Wavelength selection from a UV spectrum

Choose a monitoring wavelength.

260 nm · relative absorbance 0.92
Near λmax: strong response. Check baseline and interference.
Relative response

Best choice: strong analyte signal and a clean baseline.

CHEM 3400H

Worked example: choosing a wavelength

  • Analyte λmax: 210 nm
  • Mobile-phase cutoff: about 190 nm
  • Matrix interference: strong below 220 nm
Which wavelength should you pick?
Step 1: Check the solvent cutoff
190 nm is below 210 nm. The solvent cutoff is not the main problem.
Step 2: Check the matrix interference
The matrix absorbs at 210 nm. This could distort the analyte signal.
Step 3: Choose the compromise
Choose a wavelength above 220 nm if the analyte response remains strong enough.
CHEM 3400H
Section 02

Fluorescence, RI, and Electrochemical Detectors

02
CHEM 3400H

Fluorescence detection

  • Excite the analyte at λex.
  • Measure emitted light at a longer wavelength, λem.
  • Works for fluorescent or derivatized compounds.
Strength: very high sensitivity and selectivity for suitable analytes.
CHEM 3400H

Refractive-index detection

  • Compares column effluent with a mobile-phase reference.
  • Detects compounds with weak or no UV absorbance.
  • Common example: sugars.
Trade-off: modest sensitivity and usually limited to isocratic elution.
CHEM 3400H

Electrochemical detection

  • Applies a fixed potential at an electrode.
  • Measures current from oxidation or reduction.
  • Useful for catecholamines and some phenols.
Strength: excellent sensitivity for a narrow range of electroactive analytes.
CHEM 3400H

UV and diode-array detection

Signal

  • Measures loss of transmitted UV light
  • DAD records many wavelengths

Best used for

  • Analytes with a chromophore
  • Routine quantitative analysis
  • DAD: spectral comparison across a peak

Watch for

  • Weak response without a chromophore
  • Solvent or matrix interference
  • Peak-purity evidence is not proof
CHEM 3400H

Fluorescence detection

Signal

  • Absorb at λex
  • Emit at longer λem
  • Measure emission away from the excitation beam

Best used for

  • Naturally fluorescent analytes
  • Reproducibly derivatized compounds
  • Trace analysis

Watch for

  • Not a universal response
  • Quenching and matrix effects
  • Variable derivatization
CHEM 3400H

Refractive-index detection

Signal

  • Sample cell versus reference cell
  • Refractive-index difference gives the signal

Best used for

  • Weak or non-UV-absorbing analytes
  • Sugars and polymers
  • Isocratic separations

Watch for

  • Modest sensitivity
  • Temperature and composition drift
  • Conventional gradients are unsuitable
CHEM 3400H

Electrochemical detection

Signal

  • Oxidation or reduction at an electrode
  • Reaction current gives the signal

Best used for

  • Electroactive compounds
  • Catecholamines and some phenols
  • High sensitivity with a suitable potential

Watch for

  • Electrode fouling
  • Dissolved oxygen and mobile-phase effects
  • Gradient methods need validation
CHEM 3400H

Gradient compatibility

Usually compatible

  • UV-Vis / DAD
  • Fluorescence
  • Mass spectrometry*

Use with care

  • Electrochemical
  • Composition can change background current
  • Validate the gradient

Use isocratic

  • Refractive index
  • A gradient shifts the baseline
  • RI measures a bulk mobile-phase property
*Use MS-compatible solvents and volatile additives.
CHEM 3400H
Section 03

Mass Spectrometry Detection

03
CHEM 3400H

How LC-MS turns liquid into ions

LC capillary
high voltage
+ +
+
+
+
+
+
to mass
analyzer

Select each step.

Why an interface?
LC produces liquid. MS measures gas-phase ions.
Electrospray changes liquid effluent into ions.
CHEM 3400H

A simple picture of electrospray

  • Spray: form charged droplets
  • Dry: remove solvent
  • Release: send gas-phase ions into the MS
CHEM 3400H

What does mass spectrometry add?

  • LC: retention time and separation
  • MS: mass-to-charge ratio, m/z
  • Together: stronger evidence of identity
  • Useful selectivity for trace measurements
CHEM 3400H

LC-MS needs volatile additives

  • The mobile phase enters the ion source.
  • Use: ammonium formate or ammonium acetate
  • Avoid: phosphate and other nonvolatile salts
  • Nonvolatile residues can foul the source and reduce signal.
CHEM 3400H

Choosing an HPLC detector

  • Analyte: UV absorbance, fluorescence, or electroactivity?
  • Identity: need m/z evidence from MS?
  • Elution: gradient or isocratic?
  • Sensitivity: routine level or trace level?

CHEM 3400H
Key Takeaways

HPLC detector selection

  • UV / DAD: chromophores; DAD adds spectra
  • Fluorescence / electrochemical: high sensitivity for selected analytes
  • RI: weak UV response; isocratic methods
  • MS: m/z evidence; volatile additives
  • Choose by analyte, method, sensitivity, and confidence needed.
